questions.q: Who was Asokamitran and what was his job at Gemini Studios?
questions.a: Asokamitran (1931–2017) was a Tamil writer who worked at Gemini Studios in the 1950s; his duty was to cut out newspaper clippings on various subjects and store them in files, often writing them out by hand. A wrong answer (e.g., "he was an actor" or "he directed films") reveals the student has not grasped the author's actual role, which is crucial because his lowly position shapes his observational, satirical perspective.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the make-up department at Gemini Studios is described as an example of "national integration."
questions.a: The make-up department was headed by a Bengali, succeeded by a Maharashtrian assisted by a Dharwar Kannadiga, an Andhra, a Madras Indian Christian, an Anglo-Burmese, and local Tamils — representing multiple Indian regions and communities working together long before state-sponsored integration programs. A wrong answer that merely lists the communities without explaining the significance (e.g., "it shows diversity") misses the satirical point: the author highlights this integration in a department that turns people into "hideous crimson monsters," undermining the idealistic notion of unity.

questions.q: The author mentions "Pancake was the brand name of the make-up material that Gemini Studios bought in truck-loads." If you were to explain this to a classmate who thinks Pancake is a food item, how would you use the text to clarify?
questions.a: Step 1: Identify the sentence in the text that defines Pancake as a make-up brand. Step 2: Note the context: "Greta Garbo must have used it, Miss Gohar must have used it, Vyjayantimala must also have used it" — all are actresses. Step 3: Explain that truck-loads indicate the huge quantity used for indoor shooting under incandescent lights. Step 4: Conclude that Pancake is a heavy cosmetic, not food. A wrong answer that doesn't reference the actresses or the truck-loads shows the student cannot anchor vocabulary in textual evidence.

questions.q: Analyze why the author describes the office boy as "a bit of a poet" and how this detail contributes to the larger satire on the studio's literary pretensions.
questions.a: The office boy, in his forties, joined hoping to become a star actor, screenwriter, director, or lyricist; his failed ambitions make him resentful, and he lectures the author (who actually writes) about wasted literary talent. This irony — a failed aspirant preaching to a real writer — satirizes the studio's delusion that everyone there is a poet. A wrong answer that only says "he wrote poems" misses the contrast between his pretension and the author's genuine but unrecognized work.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's statement: "The great prose-writers of the world may not admit it, but my conviction grows stronger day after day that prose-writing is not and cannot be the true pursuit of a genius." Do you agree with his view? Justify with reference to the text.
questions.a: The author argues prose requires patient, persistent drudgery (rejection slips, resubmitting manuscripts) unlike the inspired genius of poetry. He supports this by describing his own struggle to enter a short-story contest and discovering Stephen Spender's editorship of The Encounter. A strong evaluation would note this is a humorous self-deprecation: the author himself is a prose writer (this memoir), so he undermines his own claim. A wrong answer that takes the statement literally without detecting the irony shows inability to recognize the author's tongue-in-cheek tone.

questions.q: Create a brief diary entry (50-60 words) from the perspective of the office boy on a day when crowd-shooting saves him from lecturing the author.
questions.a: "Thank god for crowd-shooting today! The giant paint vessel kept me busy slapping crimson on extras — otherwise that clerk in the French-window cubicle would have gotten another earful about his wasted talent. As if I didn't know real poetry! My lyrics would have made Vasan weep. Tomorrow I'll corner him again." A poor answer would lack the office boy's voice (resentful, grandiose) or the specific detail of crowd-shooting, indicating the student hasn't internalized the character.
